title: Finite RH certification couples local sign witnesses to an independent conserved total
claim: Across these accounts, a finite critical-line verification becomes a completeness certificate only when two representations agree: real-function sign changes supply local on-line witnesses, while an argument-principle or Turing-style count supplies the total zero population with multiplicity. The equality closes the sampling gap that either channel leaves open alone.
historical_or_program_relation: Bombieri states the abstract contour-count versus xi-sign-change logic, Moree separates localization from Backlund-style all-zero accounting, and Platt–Trudgian implement the same local-witness/global-completeness architecture at a later computational scale.
limits: This certifies only the bounded region and does not extrapolate to RH. Sign observations alone do not exclude missed, off-line, or even-multiplicity zeros, and the indexed summaries do not supply the detailed contour or Turing hypotheses needed to reproduce any run.

title: Adaptive zero searches preserve unresolved cases instead of letting throughput masquerade as proof
claim: A robust large-scale zero search is a staged decision system: cheap evaluations handle well-conditioned ordinary intervals, remainder-aware abstention routes ambiguous signs to finer evaluation or Gram-block search, and still-unresolved cases are retained for separate inspection. The exception record is part of the evidential object, not merely an implementation log.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1956 computation uses error bounds to flag and refine exceptional intervals; the 1982 program explicitly preserves plots and distinguishes shifted fallback samples from exact Gram-point statistics; the 1998 algorithm packages failures into Gram blocks and escalates numerical precision only when required.
limits: Adaptive routing improves search efficiency but does not itself provide the independent zero count required for completeness. Manual inspection is not automatic certification, shifted samples change the observable being aggregated, and none of these heuristics guarantees success on every future exceptional block.

title: Partitioning turns global analytic obligations into compatible numerical and tail certificates
claim: Both programs certify a global inequality by splitting its domain according to the strongest available representation: finite or peak-adjacent regions receive direct numerical or ordering bounds, while remote regions receive analytic decay estimates; the separately controlled pieces are then recombined into one admissibility test.
historical_or_program_relation: The Lehmer-pair computation decomposes the interaction with all other zeros into a finite local block and count-controlled tails before aggregating M+I+R. The later zero-free-region calculation similarly introduces proof-relevant breakpoints so symmetry, piecewise majorants, local numerics, and closed-form tails each govern the range they control best.
limits: The decompositions certify different quantities—a gap-environment criterion and an integral bound—and their breakpoints, constants, and error budgets are not transferable. Modular finite certification here neither proves global RH nor supplies a universal recipe for choosing an optimal partition.

title: Heuristic computation gains mathematical force only after it is compressed to a fixed witness
claim: In both polynomial searches, the optimizer or continuation path is a discovery channel rather than the final mathematical object. The intended evidential transition is to a finite witness whose relevant predicate can be checked independently: a controlled non-real-root or root-count certificate for a Jensen polynomial, or admissibility and objective inequalities for a nonnegative trigonometric polynomial.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1990 de Bruijn–Newman computation shifts from full approximate root lists toward Sturm counts, adaptive interval and precision recovery, with an explicit complex zero as secondary corroboration. The 2015 extremal search uses annealing to propose a degree-40 polynomial, after which the fixed coefficient vector—not the stochastic trajectory—is the reusable candidate certificate.
limits: The two witness predicates and verification burdens are different, so the Sturm strategy does not certify the trigonometric objective. The indexed spans explicitly leave interval-sign error control or full coefficient-and-rounding verification incomplete, and neither search establishes global optimality.

title: Scale normalization turns close zeros from isolated sightings into comparable dynamical evidence
claim: A sequence of increasingly structured normalizations changes what a small gap can support: division by the local mean spacing makes gaps comparable across height; multiplication by a global inverse-square interaction tests whether one close pair is dynamically isolated enough to certify a Lehmer condition; and a normalized consecutive-gap potential supports population-level comparison with pair-correlation statistics.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1986 computation records a rare gap after removing the leading height scale. The 1993 Lehmer calculation adds the surrounding zero field and obtains a finite deformation certificate. Rodgers–Tao later aggregate normalized gap defects and contradict the resulting equilibrium concentration with a positive density of small zeta gaps.
limits: A tiny normalized gap by itself is only finite local geometry. A Lehmer certificate still depends on controlling the full environment, while the Rodgers–Tao contradiction uses proportions and renormalized energy rather than one exceptional pair; none of these steps alone identifies the de Bruijn–Newman constant with zero.

title: Zero motion progresses from a close-pair ODE to a renormalized infinite-particle energy method
claim: The heat deformation admits a common dynamical reading in which inverse-square zero interactions drive motion, but the proof burden changes with scale. A close pair can be reduced to a gap ODE with the remaining zeros compressed into an environmental scalar; an infinite zero system instead requires finite-subsystem localization, explicit cross-boundary errors, and subtraction of a slowly varying reference lattice before a dissipative energy identity is meaningful.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1994 Lehmer-pair analysis uses the singular two-particle interaction to set the leading squared-gap scale of a threshold bound. Rodgers–Tao replace pairwise isolation by a renormalized many-body framework: localization exposes environmental defects, convex reference subtraction makes deviations summable, and controlled differentiation turns the formal Hamiltonian heuristic into approximate dissipation.
limits: The local ODE route yields pair-conditioned lower bounds, whereas the renormalized route serves a global contradiction; one is not a derivation of the other. The index does not justify transferring the pair approximation to the full system or treating approximate dissipation as exact monotonicity without its localization and domination estimates.

title: A finite verification height is a modular proof input, not a miniature global theorem
claim: Certified computation can be compressed to a bounded interface parameter and consumed by later analytic arguments without transporting the entire zero list. This makes a finite verification mathematically reusable: downstream constants, explicit prime estimates, or threshold bounds can change when the certified range meets the consuming theorem's hypotheses.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1986 account notes that a higher verified zeta range sharpens literature consequences parameterized by that height. Moree describes bounded Dirichlet-L verification entering Helfgott's unconditional analytic proof as a delimited input. Platt–Trudgian make the Riemann-zeta height H an explicit reusable parameter for prime estimates and for thresholded improvements to a de Bruijn–Newman upper bound.
limits: These interfaces concern different L-functions and downstream theorems and cannot be substituted for one another. Improvements may be thresholded rather than proportional, still require separate analytic constants and hypotheses, and never promote finite verification to global RH.

title: Critical-line specialization reduces computational cost by retaining only certificate-relevant information
claim: Factoring out the critical-line phase converts complex zeta evaluation into a real Z function, the Riemann–Siegel formula compresses that value to a short oscillatory sum with a controlled remainder, and a finite-RH run can then retain sign-change events rather than high-precision zero coordinates. Each compression is goal directed, but it shifts the main numerical risk to remainder control and the low sign margins created by close roots.
historical_or_program_relation: The 1956 method establishes the real finite-sum representation and observes that close roots with low intervening extrema are poorly conditioned for mesh detection. The 1998 analysis frames Riemann–Siegel as a square-root-time specialization with precision limits, while the 2021 verification explicitly treats sign changes as the sufficient local statistic for a count-based certificate.
limits: Faster real evaluation and sign-only storage do not certify completeness; a separate global count remains necessary. Sign changes need not reveal every multiplicity pattern, and specialization to the critical line cannot detect off-line zeros directly or extend the finite computation to an unbounded claim.
